summary: This document clarifies the RTP specification on using different clock rates within one RTP session. It also gives guidance so legacy implementations that use multiple clock rates can work with newer ones. It updates RFC 3550.

eli5.summary: Audio and video each use their own stopwatch. This explains how to keep different stopwatches in step during one call.

subtitle: Clarifies how RTP senders and receivers should handle payloads with different clock rates in one session.

tldr.problem: Some RTP implementations switch payloads, and therefore clock rates, on the same SSRC. RFC 3550 leaves the timestamp calculation unclear, so RTCP timestamps and jitter values become ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: Senders with RTCP MUST use a different SSRC for each clock rate. Senders without RTCP SHOULD do the same, or MAY keep one SSRC with a defined timestamp formula. Receivers MUST use a stated jitter formula.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 3550 with one recommended algorithm and tells legacy implementations how to interoperate with it.

facts.label: Sender with RTCP
facts.value: MUST use a different SSRC per clock rate

facts.label: Sender without RTCP
facts.value: SHOULD use a different SSRC per clock rate

today: RFC 7160 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014 that updates RFC 3550. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Clock Rate Problem
sections.content:
In RTP, the clock rate belongs to the payload format, which is identified by the payload type value. It is often the same as the sampling rate, but not always (the G722 and MPA audio codecs are examples). A sender can change payloads during a session, so the clock rate can change as well.

RFC 3550 lists multiple clock rates as a reason not to use different payloads on the same Synchronization Source (SSRC). That advice has not always been followed, which creates three problems:

  • The method for calculating the RTP timestamp is underspecified.
  • It is hard to know which clock rate applies to the RTP timestamp in an RTCP Sender Report.
  • It is hard to know which clock rate applies to the interarrival jitter in an RTCP Receiver Report.

The RFC also lists other RTCP fields that use a clock rate as a unit, such as the XR jitter fields of RFC 3611, the IJ packet of RFC 5450, the SMPTETC packet of RFC 5484 and the jitter blocks of RFC 5760.
sections.eli5: A game uses two stopwatches that run at different speeds. If you only write down "12", nobody knows which stopwatch you meant.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The clock rate is the multiplier that converts a wallclock value in seconds into an RTP timestamp value, without the fixed random offset. RFC 3550 uses several names for the same idea, including "clock frequency", "media clock rate" and "timestamp frequency".

An RTP Sender is a logical element that sends RTP packets, sends RTCP SR packets and receives reception report blocks. An RTP Receiver receives RTP packets and SR packets and sends reception report blocks.

"Legacy RTP" means RFC 3550 without the changes made by this document. Section 3 describes what legacy implementations do and is not normative. Section 4 gives the recommendations and is normative.
sections.eli5: The clock rate is how fast the stopwatch ticks. A sender talks and a receiver listens, and both write down times.

sections.title: What Legacy Implementations Do
sections.content:
The RFC describes three approaches seen in practice.

Different SSRC. Each clock rate gets its own SSRC, so there is no ambiguity in RTCP. This also seems to be the original intent of RTP. The downside is that changing the SSRC can be a problem for implementations designed for unicast addresses, where multiple SSRCs are a corner case, and lip synchronization can suffer until the first RTCP SR packet of the new stream.

Same SSRC, monotonic timestamps. The timestamp is the previous timestamp plus the capture time difference times the current clock rate. The timestamp always increases, but the jitter calculation of RFC 3550 gives an invalid result during a switch between rates, and the method depends on earlier packets that may be lost or reordered.

Same SSRC, non-monotonic timestamps. The timestamp is the capture time times the clock rate. The jitter calculation is correct, but the timestamp values can go down. RFC 3550 requires the sampling instant to come from a monotonic clock but does not say the RTP timestamp must increase. The RFC says most implementations seem to use this method, based on a survey at SIPit26 and a survey of open source implementations.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to cope. Give each stopwatch its own name tag. Or keep one name tag and keep counting upward, which confuses the scorekeeper. Or keep one name tag and let the number jump around, which the scorekeeper can handle.

sections.title: The Recommended Rules
sections.content:
Sender with RTCP. It MUST use a different SSRC for each clock rate. If the clock rate switches back to a value already seen in the stream, it MUST send an RTCP BYE and use a new SSRC. To speed up lip synchronization, the next compound RTCP packet MUST contain multiple SR packets: the first with the mapping for the current clock rate and the rest with the mappings for the other rates seen during the last period. The extension in RFC 6051 MAY also be used.

Sender without RTCP. This means RTCP is turned off by setting the RTP and RTCP bandwidth modifiers of RFC 3556 to 0. The sender SHOULD still use a different SSRC per clock rate, but MAY keep one SSRC if it calculates timestamps with a start offset. At each rate change it updates start_offset and capture_start, and the timestamp is (capture_time - capture_start) * clock_rate + start_offset.

Receiver. It MUST calculate jitter with D(i,j) = (arrival_time_j * clock_rate_i - timestamp_j) - (arrival_time_i * clock_rate_i - timestamp_i), and it MUST be able to handle a compound RTCP packet with multiple SR packets.
sections.eli5: If someone is keeping score, use a new name tag whenever the stopwatch changes. If nobody is keeping score, you may keep the same tag if you follow a careful counting rule.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: When the per-SSRC approach of Section 4.1 is used, the security considerations of RFC 3550 apply. The Section 4.2 algorithm is new, so its security properties were not considered in RFC 3550. The timestamp is still initialized with a random value, but it also depends on the current and previous clock rates, which may or may not introduce a vulnerability.
sections.eli5: The old way is known to be safe enough. The new counting rule has not been checked as carefully, so the document says so honestly.

sections.title: Example Values and Legacy Behavior
sections.content:
Appendix A has three tables of purely illustrative values. In them the clock rate moves from 8000 to 16000 and back to 8000, with packets 0.02 seconds apart. With monotonic timestamps the jitter spikes at each switch (480 and 720 in the example). With non-monotonic timestamps the jitter stays 0, but the timestamp drops from 1920 to 1120 at the last switch. The recommended method for senders without RTCP also keeps the jitter at 0.

Appendix B notes that a unified clock rate was proposed but rejected at IETF 61. Appendix C records that libccrtp 2.0.2, libmediastreamer0 2.6.0 and libpjmedia 1.0 use the non-monotonic formula, while the Android RTP Stack 4.0.3 changes the SSRC each time the format changes.
sections.eli5: The tables show that with the careless way of counting, the scorekeeper sees big jumps when the stopwatch changes. With the careful way, there are no jumps.
